replies.author: medialantern
replies.body: That is not the real number. The real number is your "actual entry price minus your slippage". And your real exist price is your "actual exit price offset by your slippage". There's a new model here very day. Sometimes 4x a day. The point is that if your model says "enter at $45.20" but you can't actually GET IN at $45.20 at the quantity you want, it's just a fun story, not a real model.

replies.author: Must_Dragonfruit
replies.body:
these are highly liquid stocks and the model only rebalances monthly, the slippage value wouldn't change the result.    
  
your point is taken: i have a few different methods that will converge/blend once i build up enough data: 

   \- \`decision\_price\`: price used by the model/agent to decide/size the trade.  
   \- \`quote\_ref\_price\`: bid/ask/mid/last from broker immediately before submit.  
   \- \`quote\_ref\_type\`: \`bid\`, \`ask\`, \`mid\`, \`last\`, etc.  
   \- \`quote\_ts\` and \`decision\_ts\`.  
  
that's why i have two brokers, ibkr and schwab, both quotes are being pulled. 

   \- \`arrival\_mid\_bps\`: fill versus NBBO midpoint at submit.  
   \- \`arrival\_side\_bps\`: fill versus ask for buys / bid for sells.  
   \- \`decision\_bps\`: fill versus model decision price.

then we execute multiple orders and compute against a quantity weighted average.

replies.author: medialantern
replies.body:
The trouble I see a lot of folks get into when trying to make automated trading algorithms is a few factors:

1. Not accounting for the trading cost. This part of slippage is commissions and other fees. It's how broker/dealers make their money, it's never zero, and if your model makes 20c on a trade but it costs you 10c on each side to get in and out you aren't profitable.

2. The bigger one is the source of the price data in back-testing. There's often a big assumption that the price you see in trading data is the price you'll actually get. It almost never is. Price data can come from trades or bid/ask values. When it comes from trades it's "late" - just because you see 200 shares go on the wire at $45.20 doesn't mean you can buy it (or sell it) at $45.20. It could have been reported late, run through a "dark pool", a snipe from a high-frequency trader picking off a sub-ms quote flashing in and out, etc. What's really going to happen is there's going to be a spread, where you've got bids at $45.17 and asks at $45.23. If you don't account for the spreads you're going to take an algo that's expecting to buy at $45.20 and it's actually going to be buying at $45.23 if you put in a market order. And if you put in a limit order, many brokers see that and will trade ahead of you. They're not supposed to but they all do it and everyone knows it.

Even if you trade stocks with 1c spreads your absolute minimum slippage from this factor is still 1c - on BOTH SIDES of the trade. It doesn't seem like much, but if your algo is expecting to get in at $45.20 and it's actually getting fulfilled higher than that, you're entering your trade "out of the money" (against what you expected). Now you can find your model is getting triggered at all the wrong spots and times because it works when you get i at $45.20 but not when you get in at $45.23.

3. Stop-loss orders can backfire. They work 100% of the time in testing tools but when you actually apply them to the market you can find that although nobody is supposed to know yours is there, they seem to anyway. The high-frequency folks have a nose for this, and they'll mess with you, pushing things around to force your orders to trigger. In stocks with very high volumes/liquidity (like the Q's) this is less of an issue, but there they have enough volatility to do it anyway. Back-testing suites don't see this because they usually look at slower data, like per-minute. But in the real market things jitter a lot and small bumps can drive people in and out of positions at spots they hadn't intended.

I could go on but my point is slippage is a real thing and a model that doesn't account for it is a bad setup. My suggestion would be to take your very simplest model, not even a profitable one, and get trading with it ASAP with a small budget. Get some real-world metrics not on how the model itself performs, but your execution platform/engine and your brokers. That's the number you really need right now.

comments.author: Expensive_Grape6765
comments.body:
Yo I just want to say that whatever you're experiencing right now can either be permanent or temporary.

I got a track record of getting from $100 to $1000 in 2 months with 200 total trades back in 2025 on any market - bearish, sideways, bullish. They are randomized entries, which means they should work on any market. And it did... temporarily.

I used that same strategy again, and it went from $1000 to <$10 with the exact same conditions and strategy.

Please do not get your hopes up over your 10% return. You need way longer time period (e.g., 1 decade) if you want to be sure.
